title: Boss: the red build
summary: A CI run is red after a refactor of invoice rounding. Read the log, fix the cause, pin it with regression tests, and replace a brittle test in review.

steps.title: Ticket BILL-412: the build is red
body: A teammate tidied up the invoice code and merged it. The nightly CI run is now red:
Test summary: total: 4, failed: 2, succeeded: 2, skipped: 0, duration: 0.4s

Two red tests, one cause? Read the values before the code: 5 pens at 0.025 is exactly **0.125**. Finance's rule is that half a cent rounds **up** (away from zero). `Math.Round(x, 2)` without a mode uses *banker's rounding* (to even), which turns 0.125 into 0.12. The second failure is the same bug seen through `Total`.
Senior habit: when several tests fail at once, look for the one cause they share before fixing them one by one.

steps.title: Fix the cause of the red build
prompt: This is the code from the merge. The CI tests (`InvoiceCiTests`, shown in the log) run against it when you press **Run checks**.
- a line costs `Quantity * UnitPrice`, rounded to the cent, **half a cent up** (away from zero);
- the invoice total is the sum of the **rounded** lines;
- a quantity of zero or less throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
Fix the bug without changing the names.
starter: public record Line(string Sku, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);
if (line.Quantity <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(line), "Quantity must be positive.");
public static decimal Total(IEnumerable<Line> lines) => lines.Sum(LineTotal);
solution: public record Line(string Sku, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);
if (line.Quantity <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(line), "Quantity must be positive.");
public static decimal Total(IEnumerable<Line> lines) => lines.Sum(LineTotal);
template: public void Plain_line_total() => Assert.Equal(7.50m, Invoice.LineTotal(new Line("mug", 3, 2.50m)));
public void Line_total_rounds_half_a_cent_up() => Assert.Equal(0.13m, Invoice.LineTotal(new Line("pen", 5, 0.025m)));
public void Total_adds_the_rounded_lines() => Assert.Equal(0.26m, Invoice.Total([new Line("pen", 5, 0.025m), new Line("clip", 1, 0.125m)]));
hints: Both failures involve 0.125. What does `Math.Round(0.125m, 2)` return, and why?
`Math.Round` has an overload that takes a `MidpointRounding` mode.
steps.explain: `Math.Round` defaults to `MidpointRounding.ToEven` (banker's rounding), which is right for statistics and wrong for this invoice rule. Money code should always name its rounding mode, so the next reader sees the rule.

steps.title: Pin it with regression tests
prompt: The fix is in. Now make sure nobody can bring the bug (or its cousins) back. This is the fixed code, compiled beside your tests:
public record Line(string Sku, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);
if (line.Quantity <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(line), "Quantity must be positive.");
public static decimal Total(IEnumerable<Line> lines) => lines.Sum(LineTotal);

Write `public class InvoiceTests` with at least **four** tests. They run against this code and four planted bugs: banker's rounding again, rounding the total instead of each line, accepting a quantity of zero, and ignoring the quantity.
A test that expects an exception: `Assert.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() => Invoice.LineTotal(new Line("pen", 0, 1m)));`

target: public record Line(string Sku, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);
if (line.Quantity <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(line), "Quantity must be positive.");
public static decimal Total(IEnumerable<Line> lines) => lines.Sum(LineTotal);

mutants.name: banker's rounding is back
mutants.hint: Test a line whose exact total ends in a half cent, such as 5 x 0.025.

mutants.name: the total is rounded instead of each line
mutants.hint: Two lines of 0.125 each: rounded per line they make 0.26, rounded at the end 0.25.

mutants.name: a quantity of zero is accepted

hints: One test per planted bug is a good start: which input shows each one?
The per-line rounding bug only shows with two or more lines that each end in half a cent.
steps.explain: The CI tests caught this regression because someone once wrote a half-cent test. Your four tests now fence the rule from every side, so the next refactor cannot quietly change it.

steps.title: Review: replace a brittle test
prompt: In code review you find this test for the late-fee rule:
It is slow, its name says nothing, and it would pass for almost any bug. The code under test:
// 14 days of grace, then 0.50 per day late, capped at 10.00.
Replace it with `public class LateFeeTests`: at least **four** `[Fact]` tests, one behaviour each, no sleeps, no loops, exact expected values. Five planted bugs are waiting.

mutants.name: late days are counted from day 1

forbid.message: No sleeps: nothing here is waiting for anything

hints: Every rule has an edge: the last free day (14), the first paid day (15), and the day the cap starts to apply.
`>= 0` passes for any non-negative bug. Assert exact values: `Assert.Equal(0.50m, LateFee.For(15));`.
For the cap, pick a day far past it (60 days would be 23.00 uncapped) and expect `10.00m`.
steps.explain: The old test had five inputs and caught almost nothing, because `>= 0` is true for nearly every bug. Four precise tests, each on an edge, catch all five. Precision beats volume.
